enrichment.short_title: Asylum judicial review after IAT leave refusal
key_facts: Manyi Tataw, a Cameroonian asylum seeker, claimed persecution including threatened female genital mutilation.
The Home Office refused asylum after she missed an interview; an adjudicator dismissed her appeal on credibility grounds.
Her application for leave to appeal to the IAT was refused as out of time because the determination was deemed served under rule 48(2)(a).
She argued she and her representatives had not received the adjudicator's determination until after requesting it on 20 July 2001.
Pitchford J refused permission for judicial review, holding the court could not interfere with the IAT decision on the material then before it.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal judicial review hearing following refusal of permission to seek judicial review of an IAT refusal of leave to appeal.
enrichment.outcome: Application for judicial review allowed; IAT refusal quashed and matter remitted for reconsideration of leave to appeal.
enrichment.ratio: Where a procedural error means an asylum applicant was denied a proper opportunity to pursue substantive grounds of appeal, the Administrative Court may quash an IAT refusal of leave even if the tribunal committed no fault on the material before it; in sensitive asylum cases the court should not refuse relief merely because an adjudicator's adverse credibility findings appear strong unless it is plain and obvious that no viable substantive appeal exists.
legal_issues: Whether the court may quash an IAT leave refusal based on facts not before the tribunal
Whether Pitchford J could address the merits of the adjudicator's decision
Whether rule 48(2)(a) deems service only at the time of the original decision
Whether natural justice required remittal in the procedural mishap

enrichment.short_title: Widowers' challenge to widow-only social security benefits

statutes_considered.title: Social Security Contributions and Benefits Act 1992

key_facts: Five widowers challenged statutory schemes paying bereavement benefits and tax allowances to widows but not widowers.
The Secretary of State accepted that paying Widow's Payment and Widowed Mother's Allowance only to women breached Article 14 with Article 8.
The court held there was no objective justification after 1995 for paying Widow's Pension to widows aged 45-65 while denying equivalent payments to widowers.
The court found post-HRA failures to make extra-statutory equivalent payments were unlawful but largely rejected monetary claims.
Only Mr Martin was awarded £1,000 damages for bereavement payment discrimination in the transitional period after the HRA came into force.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Conjoined Court of Appeal appeals from Moses J's judicial review decisions on widowers' Human Rights Act claims.
enrichment.outcome: Appeals partly allowed on discrimination and objective justification findings; declaration of incompatibility upheld for sections 36-37; monetary claims largely rejected except £1,000 damages to Mr Martin.
enrichment.ratio: Gender-based widow-only bereavement benefits constituted unjustified Article 14 discrimination once women's economic activity no longer justified differential treatment; after the Human Rights Act 1998 the Secretary of State could not rely on section 6(2)(b) to refuse extra-statutory payments needed to avoid continuing discrimination, but just satisfaction damages require demonstrated pecuniary loss and are not available merely because discrimination occurred.
legal_issues: Whether widow-only benefits breached Article 14 with Article 8 or Protocol 1 Article 1
Objective justification for Widow's Pension after 1995
Whether section 6(2)(b) HRA shielded refusal to make extra-statutory payments
Whether mandatory orders or damages should follow unlawful discrimination
Retrospective effect of the HRA and just satisfaction under section 8

enrichment.short_title: Return of seized cash under Police (Property) Act 1897
key_facts: Police seized £17,500 plus interest from a cowshed during a 1983 search linked to Kenneth Morgan's dishonesty offences.
The Court of Appeal overturned a Crown Court deprivation order because the money was not proved to be proceeds of crime.
John Rhys Morgan claimed the cash represented decades of savings by him and his late brother Thomas Morgan, coal miners.
Magistrates ordered the money paid to central funds less £5,000 costs after scepticism about the brothers' savings evidence.
Expert evidence showed John Rhys Morgan had a learning disability and kept large sums of cash at home.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of magistrates' order under section 1(1) of the Police (Property) Act 1897, pursued instead of a case stated after the 21-day limit.
enrichment.outcome: Claim allowed; magistrates' order quashed and declaration that capital and accrued interest be returned to John Rhys Morgan.
enrichment.ratio: Once police lawful authority to retain seized money is exhausted, the person from whom it was taken is entitled to possession unless another owner is established; under the 1897 Act a claimant need only show entitlement to possession and magistrates erred in treating proof of lawful acquisition as necessary where no rival claimant existed, following Webb v Chief Constable of Merseyside Police.
legal_issues: Whether judicial review was appropriate instead of case stated
Correct approach to ownership under section 1(1) of the 1897 Act
Effect of the Court of Appeal's earlier deprivation order
Whether magistrates could award money to the state on provenance doubts

enrichment.short_title: Certification of Dublin Convention human rights claims
key_facts: Three consolidated appeals concerned certification under section 72(2)(a) of human rights claims by asylum seekers facing removal to other EU states under the Dublin Convention.
Razgar, an Iraqi refused asylum in Germany, argued return there would breach Article 8 because of mental health consequences and separation from family.
The Secretary of State certified the claims as manifestly unfounded to remove appeal rights to an adjudicator.
The court held certification requires that the claim is bound to fail before an adjudicator, not merely likely or very likely to fail.
All three section 72(2)(a) certificates were quashed as not meeting that high threshold.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Consolidated Court of Appeal appeals on lawfulness of manifestly unfounded certificates for Dublin Convention removals.
enrichment.outcome: Appeals allowed; section 72(2)(a) certificates quashed in all three cases.
enrichment.ratio: A section 72(2)(a) certificate may be issued only if a human rights claim is bound to fail before an adjudicator; where Article 8(2) proportionality is in play the Secretary of State may consider justification when certifying, but the court applies anxious scrutiny and conflicting medical or factual evidence prevents certification unless the claimant's case is clearly unarguable.
legal_issues: Meaning of manifestly unfounded under section 72(2)(a)
Whether Article 8(2) may be considered at certification stage
Adjudicator's role in Article 8 proportionality review versus supervisory review
Application of Article 3 and Article 9 to removal to receiving states
Dublin Convention safe third country removals

enrichment.short_title: SEN appeal costs and child joinder refusal
key_facts: Wandsworth appealed unsuccessfully against a Special Educational Needs Tribunal decision concerning ABA provision for a child with autism.
The child's legally aided representative sought joinder as an interested party but was refused because the parent respondent could raise all issues.
After the main judgment was handed down, the representative applied for permission to appeal the joinder refusal and for costs against Wandsworth.
The court held the joinder principle followed South Glamorgan and Westminster and was not an improper interference with Legal Services Commission funding policy.
Public funding assessment was ordered for the child's representative but permission to appeal the joinder decision was refused.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Post-judgment applications following dismissal of Wandsworth's statutory appeal from the Special Educational Needs Tribunal.
enrichment.outcome: Wandsworth's appeal dismissed; permission to appeal joinder refusal refused; no order as to costs on the appeal; public funding assessment ordered.
enrichment.ratio: A child should not be joined as an interested party to a statutory SEN appeal where an existing party can raise every issue, even if public funding was obtained in the child's name; that principle reflects abuse-of-process concerns but does not constrain the Legal Services Commission's independent funding decisions.
legal_issues: Whether a child may be joined as interested party to a statutory SEN appeal
Interaction between legal aid funding and party status
Whether CPR rule 52.13 required permission for further appeal
Costs where respondent changed position during judicial review

enrichment.short_title: ABA provision in statement of special educational needs
key_facts: Wandsworth appealed a tribunal decision placing applied behavioural analysis provision in Part 3 rather than Part 4 of a child's statement of SEN.
The child A received an ABA programme funded by the LEA up to £17,136 per annum while no specialist unit placement was available.
The tribunal found ABA described facilities and staffing arrangements appropriate to meet needs specified in Part 2.
The child's legally aided counsel was refused joinder as an interested party because the mother could raise all issues.
The LEA argued Part 3 should not contain provision exceeding that necessary to meet identified needs.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Statutory appeal under section 11(1) of the Tribunals and Inquiries Act 1992 from a Special Educational Needs Tribunal decision.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; tribunal decision to include ABA provision in Part 3 upheld; application to join child as interested party refused.
enrichment.ratio: Where ABA or similar educational provision is appropriate to meet needs in Part 2 of a statement, it belongs in Part 3 as special educational provision describing facilities and staffing; temporary appropriateness because no specialist placement is available may be stated in Part 3, while Part 4 may address current placement.
legal_issues: Whether ABA provision belonged in Part 3 or Part 4 of the statement
Whether the tribunal included more provision than necessary under Surrey v P and Richardson v Solihull principles
Whether the child should be joined as an interested party
Abuse of legal aid process by funding a child as party

enrichment.short_title: Gypsy status for private caravan site planning permission

statutes_considered.title: Caravan Sites and Control of Development Act 1960

key_facts: Mr and Mrs Berry, traditional Irish travellers, settled on open countryside in Wrexham after Mr Berry's heart disease ended their nomadic life.
A planning inspector quashed an enforcement notice and granted retrospective permission for a private gypsy caravan site.
Sullivan J upheld the inspector on the basis that ill gypsies who ceased travelling could retain gypsy status for planning purposes.
Wrexham Council appealed, arguing nomadic habit of life is essential and the Inspector's reasons were inadequate.
The Court of Appeal allowed the appeals and remitted for fresh determination by another inspector.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Consolidated Court of Appeal appeals from Sullivan J on statutory challenges to a planning inspector's enforcement and permission decisions.
enrichment.outcome: Appeals allowed; inspector's decisions quashed and matters remitted for redetermination.
enrichment.ratio: For planning control, gypsy status depends on a nomadic habit of life at the date of the planning decision, not ethnic origin; traditional gypsies who have permanently ceased travelling through illness or age are outside gypsy policy, though personal circumstances may still be material considerations under sections 54A and 70(2), and an inspector must clearly identify and reason both the legal definition and the factual gypsy-status finding.
legal_issues: Meaning of gypsies in planning law and Departmental Circulars
Whether enforced retirement from travelling preserves gypsy status
Adequacy of inspector's reasons on gypsy status
Relevance of Article 8 and Chapman v United Kingdom
Material considerations when applicants are not statutory gypsies

enrichment.short_title: Admissibility of blood specimen certificate in drink-driving trial
key_facts: The appellant was stopped driving in Staffordshire, gave a positive roadside breath test, and a blood specimen showed 142mg alcohol per 100ml blood.
At trial the prosecution tendered a police surgeon's blood-taking certificate that the defence had never received before the hearing.
The magistrates admitted the certificate after the solicitor objected only once it was read out in court.
The appellant was convicted and fined £600 with 18 months' disqualification.
The magistrates stated a case asking whether the certificate and an unsigned witness statement were admissible.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal by way of case stated from Burton upon Trent Magistrates' Court after drink-driving conviction.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; conviction quashed because the medical certificate was inadmissible; PC Trow's unsigned section 9 statement was properly admitted.
enrichment.ratio: A medical practitioner's certificate under section 16(2) of the Road Traffic Offenders Act 1988 is inadmissible unless a copy was served at least seven days before the hearing; failure to serve is a bar that cannot be waived by a brief pause before objection, following Tobi v Nicholas and McCormack v DPP.
legal_issues: Admissibility of section 16(2) medical certificate without seven-day service
Whether late objection waived proof of service under Lewis v DPP
Admissibility of section 9 witness statement signed only at the top
Whether conviction could stand without the medical certificate

linked_authorities.name: Tobi v Nicholas
McCormack v Director of Public Prosecutions
Lewis v DPP

confidence.notes: Clear stated case with detailed reasoning on section 16 service requirements and conviction safety.

enrichment.short_title: Sentence for bladed article in camper van
key_facts: Police stopped the appellant driving erratically on a motorway in the early hours and found an eight-and-a-half inch knife in a scabbard on the passenger seat.
He pleaded guilty at Hull Crown Court to possession of a bladed article and received three months' imprisonment.
Two offensive weapons charges were dismissed after no evidence was offered.
He had no violence convictions but had excess alcohol driving convictions including on the same occasion.
Magistrates had already ordered 100 hours' community punishment and a three-year driving ban for the drink-driving offence.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Sentence appeal to the Court of Appeal (Criminal Division) with leave of the single judge.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed in part; three-month sentence reduced to six weeks' imprisonment.
enrichment.ratio: Where a bladed article was possessed without aggressive use and the offender had no relevant violence history, a three-month immediate custodial sentence for possession alone was manifestly excessive; six weeks adequately reflected culpability following R v Stewart.
legal_issues: Whether the custody threshold was passed
Whether three months was manifestly excessive
Appropriate sentence for passive possession of a bladed article

linked_authorities.name: R v Stewart

confidence.notes: Short judgment with straightforward facts and clear sentence reduction; section 139 inferred from bladed article offence though not explicitly cited.

enrichment.short_title: Constructive trust share for cohabiting partner in farm
key_facts: Lynette Hyett cohabited with Robert Freeman at Whitsun Brook Farm from 1988 until his death in a hunting accident in 1999.
Freeman's will left his estate to his sons; an Alba life policy was written in trust for Hyett because she would not inherit under the will.
In 1992 Hyett became joint borrower on a Barclays mortgage; Freeman assured her that with her name on the mortgage she would have a right to the property.
The trial judge found the assurance related only to relationship breakdown during Freeman's lifetime, not to his death.
The Court of Appeal held Hyett acquired an immediate absolute half share by constructive trust in March 1992 but must account for RSA mortgage protection proceeds used to repay the mortgage.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal with permission against Chancery Division judgment rejecting beneficial interest and RSA policy claims.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed in part; declaration of half beneficial interest in the farm; appeal dismissed on RSA policy proceeds claim.
enrichment.ratio: Under Rosset/Gissing principles, an express assurance that a cohabitee would have a right to property if she joined a mortgage can found a constructive trust of an immediate absolute beneficial interest; the trial judge erred in limiting that interest to survival of the relationship, and joint and several mortgage liability supports an intended half share, but a mortgage protection policy proceeds must be applied to discharge the secured debt.
legal_issues: Whether common intention constructive trust arose from 1992 mortgage assurance
Whether the assurance covered death or only relationship breakdown
Quantification of beneficial shares
Beneficial entitlement to mortgage protection policy proceeds on death
